notes: Interim Divisional Court judgment; final decision on mandatory order deferred pending Crown Court transcript.

enrichment.short_title: Renewed application for mandatory order after Crown Court dismissed drink-driving appeal
key_facts: Vivian Mary Jones was convicted in the magistrates' court of driving with excess alcohol and appealed to Guildford Crown Court.

The Crown Court adjourned for two days so three unsigned section 9 witness statements could be replaced by live evidence from Lancashire; the appeal was dismissed and she was ordered to pay £500 costs.
She sought a mandatory order requiring the Crown Court to state a case on whether the adjournment and costs orders were open to a reasonable bench.
Owen J dismissed the paper application; Brooke LJ treated the first proposed question as within Crown Court discretion and the costs question as inept without a transcript of the judge's reasons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed oral application to the Divisional Court for permission to apply for a mandatory order requiring Guildford Crown Court to state a case.
enrichment.outcome: Application not finally determined; court directed that a transcript of the Crown Court judge's costs reasons be obtained at public expense, sent to the defendant's solicitors, and further written submissions be made within three weeks before a final decision.
enrichment.ratio: Where a proposed case-stated question turns on what a Crown Court judge said when making a costs order, and both the judge and the Crown Court have indicated that a transcript is needed, it is elementary that the Divisional Court should obtain that transcript before deciding whether to require a case to be stated; an ineptly framed costs question may otherwise warrant outright dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether the Crown Court properly exercised its discretion in adjourning a part-heard appeal so prosecution witnesses could attend
Whether a case-stated question on the award of prosecution costs was properly formulated
Whether a transcript of the Crown Court judge's reasons was a precondition to adjudicating the costs question

notes: Full reserved Court of Appeal judgment on planning JR, alternative schemes, and permission-stage costs.

enrichment.short_title: Planning JR rejecting rival Oxford Street enhancement scheme and upholding permission-stage costs
key_facts: Mount Cook, freeholder of 200-212 Oxford Street, challenged Westminster's grant of operational planning permission to leaseholder Redevco for relatively minor external alterations in a conservation area.
Mount Cook had put forward alternative urban design proposals for Market Place but had not submitted its own planning application and could not compel Redevco to adopt them.
Moses J refused permission after a near full-day renewal hearing and ordered Mount Cook to pay the council's costs of £11,508.13.
The Court of Appeal retained and determined the substantive JR, holding Mount Cook's alternative proposals were not material considerations or were of negligible weight.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of permission to apply for judicial review; Court of Appeal granted permission, retained the claim, and decided it substantively.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed and claim for judicial review dismissed; Moses J's order that Mount Cook pay the council's permission-stage costs was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An alternative planning proposal is a material consideration only in exceptional circumstances and then only if there is a likelihood or real possibility of it coming about if permission is refused; where an acceptable application causes no planning harm, rival inchoate schemes need not be weighed, and a defendant who attends and successfully resists an oral permission renewal may recover acknowledgment-of-service costs under Leach but generally not attendance costs unless exceptional circumstances exist.
legal_issues: Whether a possible alternative preferable planning scheme is a material consideration under sections 54A and 70(2)
Whether operational development can be refused because it may facilitate future non-conforming change of use
Whether relief may be refused in the exercise of discretion because of the claimant's commercial motive
When costs may be awarded against an unsuccessful claimant at the judicial review permission stage

notes: Complete first-instance judgment on Article 14 ambit in council housing enforcement.

enrichment.short_title: Council tenant denied Article 14 challenge to section 189 repair-notice enforcement gap

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Lambeth secure tenant Erskine complained that unsafe kitchen socket arrangements created risk to her and her children, but extra sockets would be an improvement not a repair.
Private-sector tenants can invite the council to serve a section 189 repair notice on a landlord; a council cannot serve such a notice on itself following R v Cardiff County Council ex p Cross.
An environmental health officer considered the kitchen extremely dangerous because appliances were run from a gang socket on the cooker point.
The judge found no direct Article 8 infringement and that Part VI enforcement legislation was not within the ambit of Article 8 for Article 14 purposes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging incompatibility of Housing Act 1985 Part VI with Articles 8 and 14 ECHR.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; declaration that Parts VI and section 189(1) are not incompatible with the Convention; permission to appeal granted; costs order in favour of defendants not to be enforced.
enrichment.ratio: Article 14 applies to legislation only if it falls within the ambit of the substantive Convention right by furthering a guaranteed right in fact; Part VI of the Housing Act 1985, including section 189, was enacted to protect public health and improve housing stock rather than to promote Article 8 rights, so differential enforcement against council tenants does not engage Article 14 even where kitchen conditions are unsafe but do not directly infringe Article 8.
legal_issues: Whether inadequate electrical sockets render a dwelling unfit under section 604(1)(f)
Whether a local authority owes a direct Article 8 duty to improve socket provision
Whether section 189 enforcement asymmetry between council and private tenants engages Article 14
What test determines whether legislation is within the ambit of a Convention right

notes: Complete test-case Court of Appeal judgment on Tesco Clubcard VAT treatment.

enrichment.short_title: Tesco Clubcard vouchers held outside VAT paragraph 5 as not issued for consideration

statutes_considered.title: Sixth Council Directive 77/388/EEC
provisions: general VAT framework on consideration and supply

key_facts: Tesco's Clubcard loyalty scheme awarded points on premium purchases and, once thresholds were met, issued quarterly vouchers redeemable in store.
The VAT tribunal and High Court had disagreed whether vouchers were issued for consideration within Schedule 6 paragraph 5.
Third-party Clubcard schemes involved payments by finance houses or partners to Tesco for participation or reimbursement of points.
Points were not automatically or directly convertible into vouchers because of quarterly minima, carry-over rules, and possible removal after eight weeks without points.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law from the High Court to the Court of Appeal in a VAT test case.
enrichment.ratio: Clubcard vouchers are not issued for consideration within paragraph 5 because the grant protected by the provision is the right stated on the voucher, not the voucher itself; points earned on premium purchases are not monetary consideration for later vouchers, and an objective analysis of the whole scheme shows its economic purpose is future loyalty purchases rather than a present purchase of vouchers, following Boots, Kuwait, Primback and Hartwell.
legal_issues: Whether Clubcard vouchers fall within Schedule 6 paragraph 5 to the Value Added Tax Act 1994
Whether points or third-party payments constitute consideration in Community law
Whether tribunal findings on customer perception were relevant or legally erroneous
How to analyse loyalty schemes objectively for VAT purposes

notes: Complete compulsory purchase appeal under Acquisition of Land Act 1981 with human rights proportionality analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Owner-occupier's challenge to clearance CPO after fire-damaged Acton bungalow fails

statutes_considered.title: Prevention of Damage by Pests Act 1949

key_facts: Miss Baker had lived at 8 Westfields Road, Acton since 1968 and bought the freehold in 1999.
After a devastating 1998 fire she continued to occupy the shell-like bungalow amid rubbish accumulations and repeated public health notices.
Ealing declared a clearance area and confirmed a compulsory purchase order upheld by an inspector and the Secretary of State.
She argued less intrusive alternatives such as a section 189 repair notice had not been adequately considered and the human rights reasoning was insufficient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 23 Acquisition of Land Act 1981 against confirmation of a compulsory purchase order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Secretary of State's decision upheld; costs of £5,000 summarily assessed against the claimant; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a dwelling is indisputably unfit and poses health and environmental risks, compulsory purchase may be a proportionate interference with Article 8 and Protocol 1 rights if decision-makers properly apply the 'most satisfactory course of action' test under section 289 and explain why less intrusive measures, such as repair in default, were unlikely to succeed given the owner's lack of resources, history of non-cooperation, and absence of a credible rebuild plan.
legal_issues: Whether Circular 5/1993 paragraph 11 'last resort' test applied to Part IX clearance powers
Whether the Secretary of State gave relevant and sufficient reasons on proportionality
Whether repair or demolition notices were practical alternatives to compulsory purchase
Whether Article 14 discrimination was arguable

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment refusing fresh psychiatric evidence and additional lies direction ground.

enrichment.short_title: Murder conviction appeal dismissed over fresh psychiatry and lies direction
key_facts: Jane Andrews was convicted of murder after Thomas Cressman was beaten with a cricket bat and stabbed in his bedroom in September 2000.
At trial she relied on accident/self-defence and diminished responsibility supported by Dr Turner and Dr Gamble, but distanced herself from provocation in cross-examination.
Post-conviction reports from Dr Mason and Dr Laker diagnosed personality disorder and linked child sexual abuse history to the killing.
The jury had rejected her account of the final confrontation and the prosecution case was that she attacked a sleeping, short-sighted man out of rejection and vengeance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge; application to adduce fresh evidence and an additional ground on jury directions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all grounds; application for leave to appeal on the additional lies-direction ground refused.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh psychiatric evidence will not be admitted under section 23 where substantially similar material was available at trial and the jury rejected the appellant's account of the killing; lies directions in Richens terms are not generally required for diminished responsibility because that defence depends on medical evidence rather than the defendant's credibility, and extending the lies direction would have confused the jury.
legal_issues: Whether post-conviction psychiatric evidence should be admitted under section 23 Criminal Appeal Act 1968
Whether fresh evidence on child abuse and personality disorder could affect diminished responsibility or provocation
Whether the trial judge should have directed the jury that lies were not inconsistent with diminished responsibility

notes: Complete appeal decision quashing employment-only practising certificate condition.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor succeeds in removing employment-only practising certificate condition after late accounts
key_facts: Martin Firmin, a sole practitioner working from home after a failed firm amalgamation, repeatedly failed to lodge accountants' reports on time.
The OSS imposed a condition restricting him to approved employment/partnership and requiring an accounts course.
The Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal found breaches proved but accepted his accountant's admission of fault and made no substantive order beyond costs.
The review panel wrongly relied on wider historic complaints not put to Firmin when imposing the employment condition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Master of the Rolls under Solicitors Act 1974 section 12 against conditions attached to a practising certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; first condition removed; three-month extension granted for accounts course compliance; Law Society ordered to pay £350 plus VAT costs.
enrichment.ratio: A practising certificate condition restricting a solicitor to approved employment must be justified by the matter under decision and applied fairly; where late filing of accountants' reports is fully mitigated by an accountant's acceptance of responsibility and the SDT makes no order against the solicitor, it is disproportionate to impose an employment-only condition that would effectively end a rural sole practice.
legal_issues: Whether late delivery of accountants' reports justified an employment-only practising condition
Whether historic complaints could be relied on without fair process at review stage
What weight should be given to SDT findings of mitigation

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates may convict of common assault where self-defence force was excessive
key_facts: Mark McAuliffe was convicted at Barking Magistrates' Court of assault by beating Alison Jillions.
The magistrates were not wholly convinced by the complainant's denial that she acted in a way giving rise to self-defence.
They found McAuliffe used more force than reasonable when pushing her away.
The case stated was deficient in setting out all facts found, though sufficient to decide the point of law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Barking Magistrates' Court to the Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; answer to the stated question was yes; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates may convict of common assault where the defendant raises self-defence but the prosecution proves he used greater force than was reasonably necessary, even if they do not wholly accept the complainant's evidence and instead accept parts of each witness's account.

Whether partial acceptance of competing accounts supports a finding of excessive force in self-defence
Proper content of a case stated under Crown Court Rules 1982 rule 26(5)

notes: Complete preliminary issues judgment on bailee property insurance wording.

enrichment.short_title: Fire policy covers bailed stock only where bailee is legally liable, for full value
key_facts: Ramco and RIL claimed under an all-risks material damage policy after a Skegness fire destroyed their stock and goods bailed to them, including Ministry of Defence and third-party property.
Insurers accepted liability for property owned by the claimants but disputed cover for bailed goods.
The policy defined stock as property of the insured or held in trust for which the insured is responsible.
Goods had been bailed without fault of any claimant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on construction of section 1 of a combined all-risks insurance policy.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issues answered for insurers: cover for bailed stock responds only where the insured is liable to a third party, but then for the full value of the goods rather than merely indemnifying the insured's liability.
enrichment.ratio: In a standard material damage policy, the phrase 'held by the Insured in trust for which the Insured is responsible' limits cover to goods for which the bailee has legal liability, following Moffatt and Engel, but the section 1 obligation to pay the value of property lost or destroyed is property insurance rather than liability insurance, following Tomlinson v Hepburn and the bailee's entitlement to insure to full value under Waters.
legal_issues: Whether bailed goods are covered without legal liability to the bailor
Whether 'responsible' means legal liability or general bailee accountability
Whether section 1 provides property cover or hybrid liability cover for bailed stock

notes: Complete High Court appeal remitting customs restoration decision after Gora and Lindsay.

enrichment.short_title: Customs appeal partly succeeds and remits tobacco seizure restoration decision
key_facts: Mr Dickinson's Rover and 18kg of Golden Virginia tobacco were seized at Dover in July 2001; he contended the goods were for private use.
Customs refused restoration; the VAT and Duties Tribunal allowed his appeal after refusing a Customs adjournment and accepting his untested evidence.
Customs did not cross-examine Dickinson and stood down its witnesses after wrongly assuming an adjournment would be granted.
The High Court considered Gora on deemed forfeiture, Lindsay on proportionality in restoration, and Hoverspeed on unlawful stop and search.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 16 Finance Act 1994 against a VAT and Duties Tribunal decision on customs restoration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; tribunal's effective restoration order set aside; matter remitted to Customs to reconsider restoration on the basis goods were purchased not for profit, disregarding unlawfulness-of-seizure findings; possible condemnation notice issue left open.
enrichment.ratio: Restoration proceedings may consider whether seized goods were imported for non-profit personal or family use even where Schedule 3 deemed forfeiture prevents the tribunal re-deciding forfeiture under Gora; a review officer must apply Lindsay's proportionality analysis rather than a blanket no-restoration policy, and a tribunal may make fact findings binding on remittal where Customs chose not to challenge evidence.
legal_issues: Whether own-use evidence is admissible in restoration proceedings after deemed forfeiture under Gora
Whether Lindsay requires differentiated treatment of commercial smuggling and non-profit personal imports
Whether the tribunal erred in refusing Customs' adjournment and relying on untested evidence
Whether Mrs Dickinson's letters constituted a Schedule 3 paragraph 3 notice challenging forfeiture
